analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with flat tax credits, health savings accounts, and high-risk pools.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: Senator McCain introduced it on February 9, 2016 with a single Republican cosponsor, and the Senate Finance Committee took no action before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act — including its rules that insurers must sell coverage to anyone at standard rates — and set up a new system in its place. Individuals who buy their own insurance would get a flat tax credit that grows with age, plus expanded tax advantages for health savings accounts. States would get federal money for high-risk pools to cover people insurers won't take. At the same time, insurers could turn people away outside open enrollment and exclude preexisting conditions in certain cases, doctors would be exempt from antitrust laws when negotiating with insurers, and medical-malpractice lawsuits would face new limits.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage and get no employer help would receive a refundable tax credit (larger for older adults) even if they owe little or no tax, and any credit beyond their premium could go into a health savings account. People who use health savings accounts would get higher contribution limits, a $1,000 credit for contributions, and bankruptcy protection for the accounts. Physicians would gain an exemption from federal and state antitrust laws when negotiating with health plans, protection in malpractice suits if they follow government clinical guidelines, and new freedom to contract directly with Medicare patients. Health insurers would gain a less regulated individual market, and states would receive $1 billion per year for three years for high-risk or reinsurance pools.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Self-employed and uninsured individual-plan buyers, physicians, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for people buying their own health insurance, ranging from $900 a year for children to $3,000 a year for adults 50 and older, with any amount above the premium paid into a health savings account [S2][S3].

Raises health savings account contribution limits to match retirement-account limits, adds a $1,000 credit for HSA contributions, lets account holders roll balances to children and parents, and gives HSAs the same bankruptcy protection as retirement funds [S2][S3].
Appropriates $1 billion per year for fiscal 2016 through 2018 in grants to states for high-risk pools or reinsurance pools to subsidize coverage for people with serious health conditions [S2][S3].

Exempts health care professionals from federal and state antitrust laws when negotiating with health plans, lets Medicare beneficiaries contract directly with doctors and submit claims to Medicare, and lets doctors deduct some bad debt from providing uncompensated emergency care [S2][S3].

Changes malpractice law so that a doctor's compliance with HHS clinical practice guidelines changes the burden of proof in a health care lawsuit, and provides grants for state expert panels and health care tribunals [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions bear the biggest risk: the bill repeals the requirement that insurers sell to everyone at standard rates, and insurers may deny coverage outside open-enrollment periods and exclude preexisting conditions under certain conditions [S2]. Lower-income and older subsidy recipients could receive smaller help than the income-based credits they get today, since the replacement credits are flat amounts by age. Employees with expensive employer plans would pay more tax, because the bill caps the tax-free employer contribution at $8,000 for individual and $20,000 for family coverage. Taxpayers fund the credits and the $1 billion-a-year pool grants. Patients suing over medical harm would face a higher burden of proof when their doctor followed federal guidelines.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and patients suing over harm

drawbacks.text: Insurers could deny coverage to individuals outside open enrollment periods and exclude preexisting conditions under certain conditions, and the bill states that nothing in it creates a mandate for guaranteed issue or community rating in the private market [S2][S3].

The replacement credits are flat amounts by age rather than tied to income or local premium costs, so people with low incomes, high premiums, or expensive medical needs could end up paying substantially more out of pocket than under the current law's income-based subsidies [S2][S3].

Medicare, Medicaid, VA, TRICARE, and FEHBP beneficiaries could elect the tax credit in place of those programs' benefits, which could pull people — including those with costly conditions — out of group and public coverage into the individual market [S3].

The antitrust exemption would let physicians jointly negotiate prices with health plans, a form of collective bargaining that economists generally expect to raise what insurers and patients pay for care [S2].
Capping the tax exclusion for employer-provided coverage at $8,000 for self-only and $20,000 for family plans raises taxes on workers whose health benefits are worth more than that [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who buy their own insurance and don't qualify for much help today, the credits and expanded savings accounts would be a real gain. But the bill pays for that partly by dismantling the protections that keep coverage affordable for people who are already sick, shifting the risk of high medical costs from insurers back onto the individuals least able to bear it. The physician antitrust exemption and malpractice changes lean toward providers, not patients. On balance, the gains and losses fall on very different groups of ordinary people, and the most vulnerable would likely come out behind.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain (R-AZ), joined by Senator David Perdue (R-GA), introduced the bill in the Senate on February 9, 2016; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S3][S5].
The bill had one cosponsor, a Republican [S4].
No further action was taken after the referral to Finance — no committee vote, no floor debate, no roll call — and the bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act's protections stayed in place — most importantly for people with preexisting conditions — while the proposed tax credits and high-risk-pool grants for the uninsured never materialized. Insurers and physicians did not get the deregulation and legal shields the bill offered them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with preexisting conditions kept their protections

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 9, 2016 and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate [S1][S5].

for.name: Sen. David Perdue
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remaining eleven months of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all recorded support was Republican — McCain as sponsor with a single Republican cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill removes guaranteed-issue and community-rating requirements, lets plans deny coverage outside open enrollment, and permits preexisting-condition exclusions, while new tax credits keep routing premium dollars through insurers. The deregulation benefits insurers at the direct expense of people with costly medical needs.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: Doctors would gain an antitrust exemption for joint negotiation with health plans, malpractice protection when following federal guidelines, and freedom to contract with Medicare patients. Those shields strengthen providers' legal position relative to both insurers and patients.

industries.industry: Health savings account custodians and high-deductible plan sellers
industries.note: Higher contribution limits, a $1,000 credit, and bankruptcy protection would steer more tax-advantaged money into HSAs and the high-deductible plans that must accompany them. These tax benefits are worth most to households with income enough to save.

The bill's Small Business Health Fairness Act provisions create federally certified association health plans that pool members across employers under ERISA rules. That expands a new channel for group coverage, though such plans historically offer leaner benefits than state-regulated markets require.
